column1: # nietzsche — quotations from Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900).
# Tab-separated, two columns: quote<TAB>source.
# Same contract as lib/ukhaan.tsv: the table is the source of truth and the
# `nietzsche` CLI (modules/home-manager/tools/nietzsche.nix) is only a reader.
# TSV rather than .nix so a second consumer (neovim, waybar, a script) can read
# it with a plain split on a tab. Lines beginning with '#' are comments.
# Translations are the standard public-domain / Kaufmann-Hollingdale renderings,
# lightly normalised; the source column names the work and, where it is certain,
# the section. Quotes whose attribution could not be traced to a work were left
# out on purpose — the internet's Nietzsche is half apocryphal.
# Latin script throughout, so this one is safe on every terminal surface.
One must still have chaos in oneself to be able to give birth to a dancing star.
Man is a rope, tied between beast and overman — a rope over an abyss.
What is great in man is that he is a bridge and not an end.
I love those who do not know how to live except by going under, for they are those who cross over.
Man is something that shall be overcome.
One must be a sea to receive a polluted stream without becoming impure.
Companions the creator seeks, not corpses, not herds and believers.
There is more reason in your body than in your best wisdom.
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, On the Despisers of the Body

column1: Behind your thoughts and feelings stands a mighty commander, an unknown sage — he is called self. He lives in your body; he is your body.
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, On the Despisers of the Body

column1: Of all that is written, I love only what a man has written with his own blood.
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, On Reading and Writing

column1: Whoever writes in blood and aphorisms does not want to be read but to be learned by heart.
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, On Reading and Writing

column1: I would believe only in a god who could dance.
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, On Reading and Writing

column1: Not by wrath does one kill, but by laughter.
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, On Reading and Writing

column1: He who climbs upon the highest mountains laughs at all tragedies, real or imaginary.
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, On Reading and Writing

column1: In the mountains the shortest way is from peak to peak, but for that you must have long legs.
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, On Reading and Writing

column1: You look up when you want to be exalted. I look down, because I am exalted.
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, On Reading and Writing

column1: The state is the coldest of all cold monsters.
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, On the New Idol

column1: Everything about the state is false; it bites with stolen teeth.
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, On the New Idol

column1: Where the state ends, there begins the human being who is not superfluous.
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, On the New Idol

column1: Distrust all in whom the impulse to punish is powerful.
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, On the Tarantulas

column1: One repays a teacher badly if one remains only a pupil.
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, On the Bestowing Virtue

column1: Physician, heal yourself: then you will heal your patient too.
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, On the Bestowing Virtue

column1: Whoever cannot obey himself will be commanded.
Life is that which must always overcome itself.
Where I found the living, there I found will to power.
He who would learn to fly one day must first learn to stand and walk and run and climb and dance.
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, On the Spirit of Gravity

column1: This is my way; where is yours? For the way — that does not exist.
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, On the Spirit of Gravity

column1: One must learn to love oneself with a wholesome and healthy love.
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, On the Spirit of Gravity

column1: Courage is the best slayer: courage slays even death itself.
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, On the Vision and the Riddle

column1: Was that life? Well then! Once more!
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, On the Vision and the Riddle

column1: Man is the cruelest animal.
Only where there are graves are there resurrections.
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, The Tomb Song

column1: It is the stillest words that bring on the storm. Thoughts that come on doves' feet guide the world.
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, The Stillest Hour

column1: You must be ready to burn yourself in your own flame: how could you become new if you had not first become ashes?
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, On the Way of the Creator

column1: War and courage have done more great things than love of the neighbour.
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, On War and Warriors

column1: You should have eyes that always seek an enemy — your enemy.
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, On War and Warriors

column1: Marriage: I call it the will of two to create the one that is more than those who created it.
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, On Child and Marriage

column1: Have you ever said Yes to a single joy? Then you said Yes to all woe as well. All things are entangled, ensnared, enamoured.
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, The Drunken Song

column1: Sleep is no mean art: for its sake one must stay awake all day.
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, On the Teachers of Virtue

column1: Not when truth is dirty, but when it is shallow, does the lover of knowledge dislike to step into its waters.
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, On the Famous Wise Men

column1: The earth has a skin, and that skin has diseases; one of them is called man.
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, On Great Events

column1: The true man wants two things: danger and play.
column2: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, On Little Old and Young Women

column1: All truths that are kept silent become poisonous.
There is always some madness in love. But there is also always some reason in madness.
He who fights with monsters should look to it that he himself does not become a monster. And if you gaze long into an abyss, the abyss also gazes into you.
There are no moral phenomena at all, only a moral interpretation of phenomena.
Insanity in individuals is something rare — but in groups, parties, nations and epochs it is the rule.
The thought of suicide is a great consolation: with it one gets through many a bad night.
What is done out of love always takes place beyond good and evil.
Every profound spirit needs a mask.
Every deep thinker is more afraid of being understood than of being misunderstood.
Blessed are the forgetful, for they get the better even of their blunders.
Talking much about oneself can also be a means of concealing oneself.
Success has always been the greatest liar.
The great epochs of our life come when we gain the courage to rechristen our evil as what is best in us.
Ultimately it is our desires we love, and not the desired object.
Fear is the mother of morality.
Objection, evasion, joyous distrust and love of irony are signs of health; everything absolute belongs to pathology.
The Christian faith from the beginning is sacrifice: the sacrifice of all freedom, all pride, all self-confidence of the spirit.
Christianity gave Eros poison to drink; he did not die of it, but degenerated into vice.
He who despises himself still respects himself as one who despises.
Is life not a thousand times too short for us to bore ourselves?
The abdomen is the reason why man does not easily take himself for a god.
In revenge and in love woman is more barbarous than man.
A people is a detour of nature to get to six or seven great men.
It is not a lack of love, but a lack of friendship, that makes unhappy marriages.
God is dead. God remains dead. And we have killed him.
Live dangerously! Build your cities on the slopes of Vesuvius!
What if a demon crept after you one day into your loneliest loneliness and said: this life you now live you will have to live once more and innumerable times more?
Amor fati: let that be my love from now on. I want to learn more and more to see as beautiful what is necessary in things.
What is the seal of attained freedom? No longer being ashamed in front of oneself.
Morality is herd instinct in the individual.
Mystical explanations are considered deep. The truth is that they are not even superficial.
Thoughts are the shadows of our feelings — always darker, emptier, simpler.
Whoever knows he is deep strives for clarity; whoever wants to seem deep to the crowd strives for obscurity.
The Christian resolve to find the world ugly and bad has made the world ugly and bad.
The most perfidious way of harming a cause is to defend it deliberately with faulty arguments.
Egoism is the law of perspective applied to feelings.
Become who you are.
What does not kill me makes me stronger.
column2: Twilight of the Idols, Maxims and Arrows §8

column1: If we have our own why in life, we shall get along with almost any how.
column2: Twilight of the Idols, Maxims and Arrows §12

column1: Without music life would be a mistake.
column2: Twilight of the Idols, Maxims and Arrows §33

column1: All truly great thoughts are conceived while walking.
column2: Twilight of the Idols, Maxims and Arrows §34

column1: The formula of my happiness: a Yes, a No, a straight line, a goal.
column2: Twilight of the Idols, Maxims and Arrows §44

column1: Even the bravest of us rarely has the courage for what he really knows.
column2: Twilight of the Idols, Maxims and Arrows §2

column1: To live alone one must be an animal or a god, says Aristotle. There is a third case: one must be both — a philosopher.
column2: Twilight of the Idols, Maxims and Arrows §3

column1: Which is it: is man one of God's blunders, or is God one of man's?
column2: Twilight of the Idols, Maxims and Arrows §7

column1: Help yourself: then everyone will help you.
column2: Twilight of the Idols, Maxims and Arrows §9

column1: The bite of conscience, like the bite of a dog into a stone, is a stupidity.
column2: Twilight of the Idols, Maxims and Arrows §10

column1: Freedom is the will to be responsible to ourselves.
column2: Twilight of the Idols, Skirmishes of an Untimely Man §38

column1: One should die proudly when it is no longer possible to live proudly.
column2: Twilight of the Idols, Skirmishes of an Untimely Man §36

column1: Judgments about life, for or against, can in the last resort never be true.
column2: Twilight of the Idols, The Problem of Socrates §2

column1: The individual human being is a piece of fate.
column2: Twilight of the Idols, Morality as Anti-Nature §6

column1: One is fruitful only at the cost of being rich in contradictions.
What is good? All that heightens the feeling of power in man. What is bad? All that proceeds from weakness.
What is happiness? The feeling that power increases, that a resistance is overcome.
Faith means not wanting to know what is true.
The most common lie is the lie one tells to oneself.
In truth, there was only one Christian, and he died on the cross.
The kingdom of heaven is a condition of the heart.
Man would rather will nothingness than not will.
column2: On the Genealogy of Morals, III §28

column1: The bad conscience is an illness, but an illness as pregnancy is an illness.
column2: On the Genealogy of Morals, II §19

column1: Punishment makes hard and cold; it concentrates; it sharpens the feeling of alienation.
column2: On the Genealogy of Morals, II §14

column1: All instincts that do not discharge themselves outwardly turn inward — this is what I call the internalisation of man.
column2: On the Genealogy of Morals, II §16

column1: Convictions are more dangerous enemies of truth than lies.
There are no eternal facts, as there are no absolute truths.
Hope is the worst of evils, for it prolongs the torment of man.
There is not enough love and goodness in the world to permit giving any of it away to imaginary beings.
Many a man fails as an original thinker simply because his memory is too good.
Whoever does not have two-thirds of his day for himself is a slave.
The advantage of a bad memory is that one enjoys several times the same good things for the first time.
The best author will be the one who is ashamed to become a writer.
A joke is an epigram on the death of a feeling.
The surest way to corrupt a youth is to instruct him to hold in higher esteem those who think alike than those who think differently.
The snake that cannot shed its skin perishes. So too with minds that are prevented from changing their opinions.
A thinker sees his own actions as experiments and questions — as attempts to find out something.
I am not a man, I am dynamite.
column2: Ecce Homo, Why I Am a Destiny §1

column1: My formula for greatness in a human being is amor fati: that one wants nothing to be different, not forward, not backward, not in all eternity.
column2: Ecce Homo, Why I Am So Clever §10

column1: Nothing consumes a man more quickly than the emotion of resentment.
column2: Ecce Homo, Why I Am So Wise §6

column1: One must pay dearly for immortality: one has to die several times while still alive.
How much truth can a spirit endure, how much truth can a spirit dare?
There are no facts, only interpretations.
We have art in order not to perish of the truth.
Only sick music makes money today.
